title: The Front Reaches, the Nucleus Follows

scenes.tts: A newborn excitatory cortical neuron has no legs. It is born near the fluid-filled ventricle. Its layer lies near the outer surface, across a thick wall. Later in development, it climbs a fiber of a radial glial cell. Now imagine its front reaching forward while its nucleus stays behind. What pulls the nucleus?
scenes.visual: Cell at bottom of wall, ventricle and outer surface bars, glial fiber grows; tip reaches while nucleus stays; question mark on nucleus
scenes.narration: A newborn excitatory cortical neuron has no legs. It is born near the fluid-filled ventricle. Its layer lies near the outer surface, across a thick wall. Later in development, it climbs a fiber of a radial glial cell. Now imagine its front reaching forward while its nucleus stays behind. What pulls the nucleus?

scenes.tts: Radial glee-uh keep a long fiber running from the ventricle to the outer surface. The wall is strung with parallel fibers. A neuron born beside the ventricle can climb such a fiber. In culture, mouse neurons from the cerebellum were filmed moving along glial fibers. They moved in a stop-and-go rhythm. The tip of the cell extended and retracted out of step with the cell body.
scenes.visual: Fibres fill the wall; then the wall fades to a coverslip in culture where a neuron climbs a glial fiber in stops and goes while its tip probes out of step

scenes.tts: The forward movement of the nucleus is called nucleokinesis. It runs as a two stroke cycle. In stroke one, the leading process extends. A swelling forms in it, ahead of the nucleus. The centrosome and the Golgi move forward into the swelling.
scenes.visual: Zoom on the cell: process extends, swelling forms ahead of nucleus, centrosome and Golgi move into it
scenes.narration: The forward movement of the nucleus is called nucleokinesis. It runs as a two stroke cycle. In stroke one, the leading process extends. A swelling forms in it, ahead of the nucleus. The centrosome and the Golgi move forward into the swelling.

scenes.tts: In stroke two, the nucleus is pulled forward into the swelling. The trailing part of the cell follows. Then the cycle repeats. Think of an inchworm. The front reaches and grips. Then the back catches up.
scenes.visual: Nucleus moves into swelling, tail follows, second cycle runs against fiber ticks
scenes.narration: In stroke two, the nucleus is pulled forward into the swelling. The trailing part of the cell follows. Then the cycle repeats. Think of an inchworm. The front reaches and grips. Then the back catches up.

scenes.tts: What does the pulling? In newborn rat olfactory bulb precursors fixed mid-cycle, microtubules wrapped around the nucleus like a cage. They ran forward toward the centrosome. That cage is the track. Dye-neen is a motor that walks toward the minus ends of microtubules. Those ends sit at the centrosome. Anchored around the nucleus, dye-neen is thought to draw the nucleus toward the centrosome. Myosin two adds a second force. Where it acts is still argued.
scenes.visual: Nucleus in microtubule cage, dynein draws it toward centrosome; myosin II chip

scenes.tts: Normally the nucleus follows the front. Now break the pull. Knock down L I S one in embryonic rat cortex, and the cell body stops moving. L I S one regulates dynein. Losing one copy is enough to cause lissencephaly, a cortex with reduced folding. Now block myosin two in newborn rat olfactory bulb precursors. The leading process can keep growing while the cell body stops. The front reaches first. The nucleus is pulled after it.
scenes.visual: Three cells: normal follows; LIS1 knockdown: the cell body does not move; myosin II block: the process keeps growing but the body stops
